In brief

Half a dozen passages in the first part of Nausicaa borrow words from a 1916 novel called The Guiding Thread. There is no evidence that Joyce engaged with this work in any far-reaching way, but in a couple of instances he turned its words to interesting new uses, particularly when Gerty thinks of Bloom that "she had raised the devil in him." As both passages concern male sexual desire, they may possibly be responding to the novel's feminist outlook.

At more length

Beatrice Harraden (1864-1936) was an English novelist, playwright, and suffragist. Her first novel, a love story titled Ships That Pass in the Night (1893), sold more than one million copies. All of her works address women's rights, gender dynamics, and female personal empowerment. On a JJON page Harald Beck speculates that Joyce may have become aware of her writing when a 1917 review of his Portrait of the Artist in the Swiss periodical La Semaine Littéraire preferred his innovative writing to "les vieilles formes du roman anglais" such as "les problèmes sentimentaux de Béatrice Harraden, les méandres policiers de Conan Doyle, les niaiseries de Marie Corelli, les recherches philosophiques et sociales de Humphrey Ward." The review, Beck suggests, may have prompted Joyce to seek out Harraden's most recent novel, The Guiding Thread, which tells "the story of a country girl moulded into a Renaissance scholar of sorts by her intellectually domineering husband, but eventually breaking away from him." He copied a number of phrases from the novel into his worksheets for Nausicaa.

Some of these copyings never found their way into the chapter: "and then he left her"; "I hate you"; "bored to tears." Others contribute to its verbal texture in very minor ways: "dear old Seth" echoes in "the promontory of dear old Howth"; "she was his little Joan, his, and his only" becomes "With all the heart of her she longs to be his only." Two sentences are carried over into Joyce's prose more substantially. Harraden's "she saw that his face was strangely drawn and tired" becomes "the face that met her gaze there in the twilight, wan and strangely drawn, seemed to her the saddest she had ever seen." In a still greater appropriation, "Joan who had now come out of her rapture, laughed a joyous little laugh which had in it all the freshness of a May morning" reappears in Joyce's "The pretty lips pouted awhile but then she glanced up and broke out into a joyous little laugh which had in it all the freshness of a young May morning."

Two of the smaller borrowings seem interesting in the light of Harraden's ardent feminism. Joyce took her offhand reference to "A man of a type both coarse and garish" and turned it into a more focused indictment of men. When Gerty thinks scornfully of "the fallen women off the accommodation walk beside the Dodder that went with the soldiers," she scorns also those "coarse men with no respect for a girl's honour," displaying an assumption (or knowledge) that many men coarsely disregard women's wellbeing. A similar change is wrought on Harraden's reference to a fit of anger: "Horace was again relegated to that unimportant remoteness, [the] sense of which had roused the devil in him." Nausicaa gives the expression a more sexual and gender-specific meaning when Gerty sees Bloom eying her "as a snake eyes its prey. Her woman's instinct told her that she had raised the devil in him and at the thought a burning scarlet swept from throat to brow." The devil here is predatory sexual desire, which inheres in male nature. Snakes are not only predatory but also phallic, and by changing "roused" to "raised" Joyce makes the association impossible to overlook.

Beck remarks, "Once again we can see that Joyce was always alert for the mot or phrase juste, and cared little for the contexts of his finds in their sources." As a characterization of his borrowings from authors like Homer and Dante, this assertion could not be more wrong. Perhaps it is true of some lesser writers, and perhaps Harraden is one of them, but Joyce's skill at insinuating intertextual dialogue inclines me always to listen for possible echoes of a source's "contexts." In this instance, the sharp sexual edge that he imparts to "coarse" and "rouse the devil" may indicate that Gerty feels some affinity for early 20th century feminist arguments.

John Hunt 2026
